newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sturdy in late Europe, spotlight on crosses.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sturdy in late Europe, spotlight on crosses.

text.p: The dollar ended the European session little changed on the day as the market spotlight again fell on European monetary union developments.

A row erupted between Italy and France just two days before their summit in Naples after French President Jacques Chirac suggested Italy might not make the first wave of countries to form a single currency. The mark spiked up against the Italian lira before beating a hasty retreat.
Newly-released U.S. data had little impact on the dollar. Analysts said the market's real preoccupation was with Friday's all-important non-farm payrolls figures for September.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5265/70 marks by 1541 GMT, near its session high and unchanged from late Monday's European level.

"We've had this break above 1.52 and I think people feel it can be sustained above there short-term but are not really willing to take it beyond that because they're uncertain about how the dollar will react to Friday's figures," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase Investment Bank.
Dollar/yen was quoted at 111.38/41 versus yesterday's close of 111.55/65.
The mark's generally soft tone is a major support for the dollar at present, Gunner said. "It's difficult to argue that there's any independent dollar strength around at the moment."

Dollar/yen took heart after a Japanese Ministry of Finance official said Finance Minister Wataru Kubo's overnight remark that he supported a "strong' and not necessarily "stronger' dollar did not mean the government opposed a higher dollar/yen.

On the U.S. data front, the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index for September fell more than expected, to 51.7 from August's reading of 52.6. The market had been expecting 52.5 on average.

However, analysts noted that the prices component rose to 51.2 from 47.4 in August. That echoed the Chicago Purchasing Managers' Index for September released yesterday, in which the overall index fell to 56.3 from August's 60.0 but the prices paid component jumped to 59.3 from 51.8.
"The prices components of the purchasing managers' indices have been particularly noticeable,"said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ here.
"They're not doing huge damage to the market but it's a sign the U.S. needs to put its interest rates up as a safety measure," he added.
U.S. August leading indicators showed a 0.2 percent rise, in line with market forecasts and unchanged from July.
In Rome, political sources said Italy almost called off its Naples summit with France on October 3-4 after Chirac cast doubt on whether Italy would be in the first group of EMU countries.
One source said the summit was "about to be scrapped" before Chirac issued a subsequent statement saying he ardently hoped Italy would succeed in joining EMU from 1999.
Italy had spoken darkly of French "grave interference", with Prime Minister Romano Prodi summoning France's ambassador to Italy, for an explanation of Chirac's original remarks.
But analysts said the market had remained pretty unfazed.
""The Italians got more excited than the bond market has," said Chase's Gunner.
The lira dipped through the 1,000 per mark level immediately after the Franco-Italian spat broke out, but recovered to 998.40/90 by 1614 GMT compared to late Monday's level here of 997.90/8.20.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8968
